detail:
StatPearls states that, as compression of the celiac artery is believed to be the primary pathology in celiac artery compression syndrome, therapy is directed at the release of this compression. There is no known medical treatment of celiac artery compression syndrome. As first-line therapy, the surgical division of the median arcuate ligament can be performed in two ways: traditional open surgery, or with the use of minimally invasive techniques. The minimally invasive approach can involve laparoscopy or the use of a robot, and its main advantage is described as a shorter hospital stay, improved pain control, smaller incisions, and avoidance of postoperative wound complications.

The division of the ligament is often combined with neurolysis of the celiac nerve plexus, which may contribute to improved symptom relief. In selected patients, additional procedures described include celiac artery bypass, balloon angioplasty with or without stenting, and para-spinal ganglion nerve blocks, with angioplasty and stenting typically reserved for refractory cases where first-line surgical therapies have not provided relief. StatPearls reports that following surgical intervention, about 60% to 70% of patients report symptom relief.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about median arcuate ligament syndrome treatment.
summary: StatPearls describes treatment of celiac artery compression syndrome as directed at release of the compression, states there is no known medical treatment, and names surgical division of the median arcuate ligament as first-line therapy, performed by traditional open surgery or minimally invasive techniques.
takeaways: there is no known medical treatment, statpearls states
treatment aims at releasing the compression of the celiac artery
first-line therapy is surgical division of the ligament, open or minimally invasive
about 60 to 70 percent of patients report symptom relief after surgery
title: Median arcuate ligament syndrome: releasing the compression
